newsitem.title: THAILAND: Child trafficking said big problem in Mekong area.
newsitem.headline: Child trafficking said big problem in Mekong area.

text.p: Child trafficking is a growing problem in Southeast Asia and coordination is needed to stem the flow of minors forced across borders to work -- often as bonded labourers or prostitutes, experts said on Thursday.
"Today we are here for the region's children," said Srisak Thaiarry, head of Child Rights ASIANET, which organised a three-day conference of regional law officials.
"We all know about trafficking. But there is still much to be learned and even more to be done," Srisak said. "Solid monitoring and enforcement mechanisms must be put in place."
Child rights experts told the conference that Thailand was the major recipient of children who are trafficked from nations in the Mekong River region.

"Children come to Thailand from Laos, Burma, Cambodia, China and Vietnam," said Khemporn Wiroonrapan, director of the Foundation for Child Development. "They become prostitutes, child workers, beggars or street children."
She said children from Vietnam are also trafficked to Cambodia or China and some from Cambodia or south Asian nations are moved through Thailand to Malaysia.
Khemporn said there were more than 100,000 children under the age of 18 from neighbouring countries who are working in Thailand.
She said statistics for the exact number of trafficked children were not available, but said a recent study done by Thailand's Mahidol University showed it was on the rise.
"This is due to push factors from neighbouring countries and growing demand in the receiving nations," she said. "Trafficking in children is a big money maker."

Children from rural areas or countries where there is little employment opportunity often were lured into prostitution or slave-like labour by middlemen working as job placement agents. The "agents" were often part of bigger, organised groups.
They waited in border areas to recruit children wanting to leave their country and seek work where they think life will be better, the experts said.
The children were often forced to work in the new country as bonded labourers to repay "agents" under conditions tantamount to slavery, said Amor Almagro of Child Rights ASIANET.
Topics at the conference also included how to repatriate children when and if they are discovered.
Often those who are repatriated have difficulty fitting back into life in their homeland -- especially for those involved in the sex industry.

"Some of them are just dropped off at the border and told to go home, but they don't know how to go home. So they end up back at the border again and traffickers bring them back into the country again," said Khemporn.
